all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: extended reality
concepts.definition: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

concepts.name: lighting
concepts.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

defining_facts.text: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

concepts.name: graphics processing unit
concepts.definition: A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).

defining_facts.text: A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).
A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the hardware component that is used for speeding up the rendering process.

In a typical virtual reality (VR) system that uses a game engine as middleware, the layers from lowest to highest are hardware, rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), game engine, and application software, and the hardware layer includes a graphics processing unit (GPU), a central processing unit (CPU), and memory.

An audio engine can perform its calculations on a central processing unit (CPU) or on a dedicated application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), so it does not require a graphics processing unit (GPU), and audio engines are not typically associated with a GPU because a GPU is generally associated with graphics or rendering.

A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the processing unit of a separate graphics card, with its own memory elements, that is used in computer graphics and virtual reality to exploit the inherent parallelism of graphics operations, which are highly parallel, whereas central processing units (CPUs) are generally not designed for large-scale parallel activities, although modern CPUs have some parallel features.

A GPU is typically a multicore system in which many cores, each capable only of simple integer and floating-point arithmetic, work simultaneously on one single instruction and produce data simultaneously, and groups of cores form streaming multiprocessor units, each containing several cores.

A GPU is broadly organized with a host, input assemblers and a thread execution manager, where the manager allocates work to many streaming multiprocessors, each of which has a parallel data cache, and a texture storage stores predefined surface colors, with the elements exchanging data with global memory through load and store information.

The GPU performs modeling transformation by applying transformations such as rotation, multiplying the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously for all vertices, producing a stream of transformed triangles from local coordinates to world coordinates, which gives a significant performance gain in real-time rendering because millions of vertices need to be processed per second and even more for a realistic immersive experience.

Most graphics systems assume that a scene to be rendered is made of triangles, so surfaces are converted into triangular meshes regardless of how a developer defines an object, and the GPU assumes such a mesh as input.
Graphics libraries provide application programming interfaces (APIs) through which triangles in a mesh are sent to the GPU one vertex at a time, and the GPU assembles the vertices into triangles.
The GPU computes vertex color by performing vector dot products, as in the simple lighting model, simultaneously for multiple vertices.

The GPU projection stage combines viewing transformation, projection transformation and viewport transformation in a composite matrix multiplied with vertices, producing a stream of triangles in screen or device coordinates, a continuous coordinate space, ready to be converted to pixels.

In rasterization, the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles are determined, and algorithms exploit the fact that each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels so that the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously in parallel.
In the GPU pixel processing stage, the two activities that take place are surface texturing and hidden surface removal.

In the pixel processing stage, the simplest surface texturing method applies stored texture images to the geometry being rendered by replacing the computed pixel color with the texture color at the corresponding texture point; GPUs store textures in high-speed texture storage on the graphics card, which each pixel calculation must access, and because nearby pixels tend to access nearby texture image locations, specialized memory caches reduce access time.

concepts.name: scene
concepts.definition: The Unity scene view is the developer's interactive view of the scene being created, and it shows the scene while it is being built and lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects, which are the fundamental concepts in Unity, that together comprise the scene.

defining_facts.text: The Unity scene view is the developer's interactive view of the scene being created, and it shows the scene while it is being built and lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects, which are the fundamental concepts in Unity, that together comprise the scene.
The Unity game view is the final view used to preview a developed scene, and it renders the scene from the camera set by the developer to represent the final published or deployed application.

concepts.name: platform
concepts.definition: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

defining_facts.text: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

Deployment of a virtual reality (VR) application can be native application deployment, which requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, or web application deployment, which allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.
In deployment, a platform typically means the operating system (OS) plus the hardware, with Windows or Mac OS for desktop platforms and Android or iOS for mobile platforms.

A software development kit (SDK) is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating system (OS) combination, providing fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual reality (VR) experiences for specific platforms.

Native deployment software development kits (SDKs) can be categorized in two ways: by application type, as virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) applications, and by availability, as proprietary or open source.

concepts.name: light source
concepts.definition: A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived.

defining_facts.text: A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived.
In the simple lighting model, the diffuse light component is light that comes directly from a light source and is reflected in a diffuse manner from the surface.
In the simple lighting model, the specular reflection component is light that comes from a light source and is reflected with a specular effect, producing a shiny bright spot.

concepts.name: application programming interface
concepts.definition: A computer graphics (CG) programmer does not always need to implement the stages of a graphics pipeline from scratch; instead, the programmer can import graphics libraries and use the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by those libraries to deal with the lower-level tasks, choosing a library whose APIs suit the requirements.

defining_facts.text: A computer graphics (CG) programmer does not always need to implement the stages of a graphics pipeline from scratch; instead, the programmer can import graphics libraries and use the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by those libraries to deal with the lower-level tasks, choosing a library whose APIs suit the requirements.
The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries are predefined sets of functions that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, perform specific tasks.

The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries eliminate the need for a programmer to know every detail of the underlying system or platform, such as processor details, memory details, and operating system details, in order to build a graphics application.

concepts.name: node
concepts.definition: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.

defining_facts.text: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.

In a scene-graph representation of the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, the whole activity is represented as a node graph containing nodes for video input, tracking, a root node, a virtual camera whose parameters can be manipulated, projection, other related concepts, the three-dimensional (3D) object, and transformations represented as a single node or individual nodes; video input comes from the input device, tracking uses device sensors such as a camera, and graphics-rendering nodes include transformation, three-dimensional (3D) object representation, and orthographic projection, making the scene easier to visualize and manipulate to create the desired effect.
In the virtual reality path optimization model, each node has two associated quantities: importance and waiting time.

In the virtual reality path optimization formulation, the waiting time at a node, which is a point of interest, is the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node, and it is represented by a waiting-time function W that maps each node v in V to a positive real number.
For a path P with vertices v1 to vn, the total waiting time W(P) is the sum of the individual waiting times W(v_i) for i = 1 to n.

concepts.name: three-dimensional graphics pipeline
concepts.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.

defining_facts.text: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.
The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.
The first stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, object representation, defines the objects that together form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system.

The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene.

The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, scan conversion, transforms the continuous device coordinate system description, whose points can take real-number coordinates, into the discrete pixel-grid or screen coordinate system, where each pixel coordinate is an integer.

Transforming an object definition to a pixel-level scene description in the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline uses six coordinate systems: the local coordinate system, the world coordinate system, the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, the device coordinate system, and the pixel-grid or screen coordinate system.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline consists of five stages in order: object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling transformation, which transforms a local coordinate description to a world coordinate description; lighting, which takes place in the world coordinate reference frame; the viewing pipeline, which contains viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to a three-dimensional view coordinate system, clipping in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; and scan conversion, which transforms the device coordinate scene description to a screen coordinate or pixel grid description.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline has five stages, and the first four stages are object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling or geometric transformation from the local coordinate system to the world coordinate system; lighting in the world coordinate system; and viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

In the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, after the viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the scan conversion stage, also called the rendering stage, which transforms a device coordinate description into a screen coordinate description on the pixel grid.

concepts.name: Unity
concepts.definition: Unity is a popular and well-known programming environment for developers who wish to work with extended reality systems.

defining_facts.text: Unity is a popular and well-known programming environment for developers who wish to work with extended reality systems.
The Unity platform comprises the Unity three-dimensional (3D) game engine and a developer's interface that a developer can use to implement ideas.

The Unity platform is intended to provide implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, including object definition, scene construction, lighting effects, view transformation, and scan conversion or rendering, so that a developer can focus on building the immersive experience rather than mastering and implementing the pipeline.
Unity is a cross-platform game engine that Unity Technologies initially released in 2005.

Unity supports both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) games or interactive content, and it supports over 20 different platforms, including personal computer (PC), mobile, Android-based mobile, and Apple's iOS mobile platform.

concepts.name: graphics pipeline
concepts.definition: The graphics pipeline is the set of the distinct stages in which the color values stored in the frame buffer are computed.

defining_facts.text: The graphics pipeline is the set of the distinct stages in which the color values stored in the frame buffer are computed.

concepts.name: mesh
concepts.definition: Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

defining_facts.text: Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

Objects with non-polygonal surfaces can be represented using mesh representation by approximating the surfaces with polygonal meshes, typically triangles, although other simple convex polygons may also be used.
A Unity model file can contain mesh, material, and texture data, and, if the object represents an animated character, it can also contain animation-related data.

In Unity, three-dimensional (3D) meshes are the main graphics primitives, and Unity supports triangulated or quadrangulated polygonal meshes, meaning meshes whose polygons are triangles or quadrangles.
In Unity's mesh rendering workflow, the mesh renderer takes geometry from the mesh filter and renders it at the position defined by the game object's transform component.

In a Unity model file, materials describe the appearance of an object's surface by specifying how the surface should be rendered, including references to textures used, tiling information, color tints, and other information, whereas meshes describe the object's shape.

In Unity, textures are bitmap images applied over a mesh surface as a way to assign colors to the surface, and they can represent many other aspects of a material's surface in addition to basic color, such as reflectivity and roughness.

concepts.name: unity editor
concepts.definition: Unity Hub is a standalone application that is the primary way to install the Unity Editor and the Unity Game Engine; installing Unity Hub gives the Unity Editor interface and the Unity Game Engine and streamlines finding, downloading, and managing Unity projects and installations.

defining_facts.text: Unity Hub is a standalone application that is the primary way to install the Unity Editor and the Unity Game Engine; installing Unity Hub gives the Unity Editor interface and the Unity Game Engine and streamlines finding, downloading, and managing Unity projects and installations.

The Unity Editor interface is essentially an integrated development environment (IDE) whose menu options provide developers the features required to build and deploy a system, and it allows developers to build and deploy realistic immersive environments without having to master and implement the computer graphics (CG) pipeline.
Unity Hub installation is not mandatory; the Unity Editor and the Unity Game Engine can be installed separately, and in that case the developer can deal with only one version of Unity.

concepts.name: component
concepts.definition: A Unity scene is a specific type of Unity asset that contains all or part of a game or application, and a scene can comprise components, each of which can be a different asset.

defining_facts.text: A Unity scene is a specific type of Unity asset that contains all or part of a game or application, and a scene can comprise components, each of which can be a different asset.

A Unity game object is a fundamental object that represents characters, props, or a scenario and acts as a container for components that implement the object's functionality, so its properties are given by adding components to it.

Built-in component types can be assigned to Unity game objects through the Unity editor interface, and custom components and game objects can be created using scripting application programming interfaces (APIs).

never_defined.name: three-dimensional space
never_defined.definition: In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

never_defined.name: geometry
never_defined.definition: The geometry and terrain of a virtual environment affect cybersickness (CS); when a user travels over regular bumps and irregular terrain, CS is more likely than when the same travel occurs over flat terrain without bumpy rides.

never_defined.name: camera
never_defined.definition: In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems.

never_defined.name: point
never_defined.definition: In natural feature tracking, the advanced image processing algorithms or computer vision techniques detect features that are unique to the surroundings with respect to the object to be tracked, such as points, corners, and line intersections.

never_defined.name: force
never_defined.definition: A completely synthetic virtual world requires defining a triangular mesh in a three-dimensional space and maintaining material and physical surface properties that indicate how the surfaces interact with light, sound, and forces.

never_defined.name: gravity
never_defined.definition: Physics support in a virtual world generator should make a dropped ball accelerate toward the ground due to gravity rather than move it at constant speed.

never_defined.name: collision
never_defined.definition: Collision support in a virtual world generator should ideally include collision detection, which determines whether two or more bodies intersect, and collision response, which determines how they should behave after a collision occurs.

never_defined.name: surface
never_defined.definition: Physics support in a virtual world generator should also replicate other physical-world phenomena, such as how light propagates, how light interacts with different surfaces, the effects generated, the sources of light and resulting illumination effects, and how sound and smell propagate.

never_defined.name: resource requirement
